BM25 outperforms gradient-based and embedding-based TDA methods on the FTRACE-TREX dataset with real facts.
On the synthetic FTRACE-SYNTH dataset, TDA methods perform better, especially when lexical overlap is reduced.
Gradient normalization and the use of Adafactor accumulators significantly improve TracIn performance.
The embedding layer provides the most reliable attribution signal for both gradient and embedding-based methods.
There is substantial headroom for improving TDA methods for fact tracing, as they do not yet reliably outperform model-agnostic baselines.
papers.limitation:
Gradient saturation can cause TDA methods to fail when the model's loss is already zero at the start of the training period monitored.
Lexical overlap between queries and training examples can confound attribution methods, favoring simple IR baselines.
future_direction: Overcoming the problem of gradient saturation
Improving TDA methods to handle lexical variation in fact expression
Developing more accurate and scalable fact tracing techniques
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) have been shown to memorize a great deal of factual knowledge contained in their training data. But when an LM generates an assertion, it is often difficult to determine where it learned this information and whether it is true. In this paper, we propose the problem of fact tracing: identifying which training examples taught an LM to generate a particular factual assertion. Prior work on training data attribution (TDA) may offer effective tools for identifying such examples, known as "proponents". We present the first quantitative benchmark to evaluate this. We compare two popular families of TDA methods -- gradient-based and embedding-based -- and find that much headroom remains. For example, both methods have lower proponent-retrieval precision than an information retrieval baseline (BM25) that does not have access to the LM at all. We identify key challenges that may be necessary for further improvement such as overcoming the problem of gradient saturation, and also show how several nuanced implementation details of existing neural TDA methods can significantly improve overall fact tracing performance.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Persuade? Linear Probes Can Uncover Persuasion Dynamics in Multi-Turn Conversations
papers.research_question: How do LLMs persuade in multi-turn conversations? The paper investigates using linear probes to uncover persuasion dynamics, including persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for analyzing persuasion dynamics in LLM-driven conversations using linear probes, demonstrating that these lightweight probes can efficiently capture key aspects of persuasion (outcome, strategy, personality) and match or outperform prompting-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes are a promising, efficient tool for studying complex behaviors like persuasion in multi-turn LLM conversations, enabling fine-grained analysis at scale and offering insights into persuasion dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can accurately identify where persuasion success or failure occurs in a conversation, detect rhetorical strategies, and estimate persuadee personality.
Probes are computationally much more efficient than prompting-based methods, especially for fine-grained, multi-turn analysis.
Persuasive cues concentrate around the middle turns in human-human dialogues but shift to the final turns in synthetic LLM-generated dialogues.
Probe outputs reveal correlations between personality traits (e.g., extraversion) and the effectiveness of different rhetorical strategies.
Probes can perform as well as or even outperform prompting in some settings, such as uncovering persuasion strategy.
future_direction: Applying the probing approach to study other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation.
Scaling the approach to larger models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have started to demonstrate the ability to persuade humans, yet our understanding of how this dynamic transpires is limited. Recent work has used linear probes, lightweight tools for analyzing model representations, to study various LLM skills such as the ability to model user sentiment and political perspective. Motivated by this, we apply probes to study persuasion dynamics in natural, multi-turn conversations. We leverage insights from cognitive science to train probes on distinct aspects of persuasion: persuasion success, persuadee personality, and persuasion strategy. Despite their simplicity, we show that they capture various aspects of persuasion at both the sample and dataset levels. For instance, probes can identify the point in a conversation where the persuadee was persuaded or where persuasive success generally occurs across the entire dataset. We also show that in addition to being faster than expensive prompting-based approaches, probes can do just as well and even outperform prompting in some settings, such as when uncovering persuasion strategy. This suggests probes as a plausible avenue for studying other complex behaviours such as deception and manipulation, especially in multi-turn settings and large-scale dataset analysis where prompting-based methods would be computationally inefficient.

papers.title: Unveiling LLMs: The Evolution of Latent Representations in a Dynamic Knowledge Graph
papers.research_question: Which factual knowledge do LLMs use to assess input truthfulness? How does this knowledge evolve across layers? Are there any distinctive patterns in its evolution?
papers.core_contribution: An end-to-end framework that decodes factual knowledge from LLM latent representations (as ground predicates) and represents its layer-wise evolution as a dynamic knowledge graph, enabling local and global interpretability analyses.
papers.conclusion: By decoding semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this framework advances our understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process and the mechanistic interpretability of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Entity centrality is highlighted in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluations.
The global analysis reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts.
Early layers focus on syntax and entity resolution, while middle layers are crucial for factual knowledge resolution.
The framework can identify representation errors, such as entity confusion, duplication, and example leakage, that lead to incorrect evaluations.
The model's classification performance shows an imbalance, with higher precision for true claims and higher recall for false claims on FEVER, and more balanced recall on CLIMATE-FEVER.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive capacity to recall a vast range of factual knowledge. However, understanding their underlying reasoning and internal mechanisms in exploiting this knowledge remains a key research area. This work unveils the factual information an LLM represents internally for sentence-level claim verification. We propose an end-to-end framework to decode factual knowledge embedded in token representations from a vector space to a set of ground predicates, showing its layer-wise evolution using a dynamic knowledge graph. Our framework employs activation patching, a vector-level technique that alters a token representation during inference, to extract encoded knowledge. Accordingly, we neither rely on training nor external models. Using factual and common-sense claims from two claim verification datasets, we showcase interpretability analyses at local and global levels. The local analysis highlights entity centrality in LLM reasoning, from claim-related information and multi-hop reasoning to representation errors causing erroneous evaluation. On the other hand, the global reveals trends in the underlying evolution, such as word-based knowledge evolving into claim-related facts. By interpreting semantics from LLM latent representations and enabling graph-related analyses, this work enhances the understanding of the factual knowledge resolution process.

papers.title: Seeing but Not Believing: Probing the Disconnect Between Visual Attention and Answer Correctness in VLMs
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether VLM failures in visual question answering arise from not perceiving the visual evidence or from not effectively leveraging the perceived evidence.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that VLMs often attend to correct evidence even when answering incorrectly ('seeing but not believing') and introduces VEA, a training-free inference-time method that uses deep-layer attention to highlight evidence regions, improving answer accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals that attention transitions from text to image across layers, deep layers act as visual grounders, and models often see but not believe; the introduced VEA method leverages deep-layer attention to highlight evidence and improves factual answering without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers focus primarily on text tokens, while deeper layers progressively shift attention to image tokens.
Deep layers sparsely but reliably attend to localized evidence regions, acting as visual grounders.
VLMs often perceive the correct visual evidence even when outputting incorrect answers, a phenomenon termed 'seeing but not believing'.
The proposed VEA method, which highlights deep-layer evidence regions, consistently improves answer accuracy across multiple VLM families without training.
VEA's evidence attribution aligns well with ground-truth evidence, as measured by AUROC and NDCG.
papers.limitation:
Relies on extracting attention maps, which may not be supported by proprietary or API-only VLMs.
Attention may not fully capture all internal mechanisms of evidence localization; alternative attribution signals could provide complementary insights.
Per-model profiling, while effective, could be made more efficient for large-scale or real-time applications.
future_direction: Using attention signals to guide dynamic image manipulations (e.g., cropping or zooming) for complex reasoning tasks.
Combining attention with lightweight enhancement modules (e.g., super-resolution) for self-triggered visual enhancement.
Embedding self-directed evidence gathering into agentic frameworks for active problem solving.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong results on multimodal tasks such as visual question answering, yet they can still fail even when the correct visual evidence is present. In this work, we systematically investigate whether these failures arise from not perceiving the evidence or from not leveraging it effectively. By examining layer-wise attention dynamics, we find that shallow layers focus primarily on text, while deeper layers sparsely but reliably attend to localized evidence regions. Surprisingly, VLMs often perceive the visual evidence when outputting incorrect answers, a phenomenon we term ``seeing but not believing'' that widely exists in major VLM families. Building on this, we introduce an inference-time intervention that highlights deep-layer evidence regions through selective attention-based masking. It requires no training and consistently improves accuracy across multiple families, including LLaVA, Qwen, Gemma, and InternVL. These results show that VLMs encode reliable evidence internally but under-utilize it, making such signals explicit can bridge the gap between perception and reasoning, advancing the diagnostic understanding and reliability of VLMs.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: From Passive to Persuasive: Steering Emotional Nuance in Human-AI Negotiation
papers.research_question: Whether complex social behaviors, such as empathy and strategic politeness, are encoded as localized, approximately linear directions in LLM activation space and can be effectively steered via attribution-guided activation injection.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces STAR, a two-stage inference-time framework that uses attribution patching to localize where behavioral traits causally originate and injects contrastive activation vectors at those positions. It demonstrates that complex interpersonal behaviors are encoded as localized, linear directions in activation space and can be effectively steered.
papers.conclusion: The findings indicate that complex interpersonal stances are recoverable as precise, localized directions in residual stream space, and that the central challenge in behavioral alignment is identifying where behavioral intent is encoded, not model capacity.
papers.key_findings:
Localized activation injection (STAR) consistently outperforms global steering and instruction priming across emotional dialogue and negotiation tasks.
Steering effects persist and can compound across multi-turn interactions, with larger effect sizes than in single-turn settings.
Human evaluation confirms that automatic metric gains reflect genuine improvements in perceived conversational quality, not superficial lexical changes.
Attribution patching reveals that behavioral traits localize to specific early-layer attention and MLP components, with distinct patterns for affective vs. strategic tasks.
The work challenges the assumption that complex, context-dependent social behaviors resist linear decomposition in activation space.
papers.limitation: Failure modes include verbatim self-repetition, context mismatch, and register over-inflation where affective framing is applied disproportionately.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate increasing conversational fluency, yet instilling them with nuanced, human-like emotional expression remains a significant challenge. Current alignment techniques often address surface-level output or require extensive fine-tuning. This paper demonstrates that targeted activation engineering can steer LLaMA 3.1-8B to exhibit more human-like emotional nuances. We first employ attribution patching to identify causally influential components, to find a key intervention locus by observing activation patterns during diagnostic conversational tasks. We then derive emotional expression vectors from the difference in the activations generated by contrastive text pairs (positive vs. negative examples of target emotions). Applying these vectors to new conversational prompts significantly enhances emotional characteristics: steered responses show increased positive sentiment (e.g., joy, trust) and more frequent first-person pronoun usage, indicative of greater personal engagement. Our findings offer a precise and interpretable framework and new directions for the study of conversational AI.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: Do Personality Traits Interfere? Geometric Limitations of Steering in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether personality steering directions are geometrically independent in large language models, what happens to steering effectiveness when geometric independence is explicitly enforced, and if observed trait dependencies are consistent across different model families.
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering directions in LLMs are not geometrically independent; enforcing orthogonality does not eliminate cross-trait behavioral effects and can reduce steering strength and fluency, indicating that traits occupy a coupled subspace.
papers.conclusion: Personality traits in large language models are not independent directions in activation space, and geometric constraints on steering vectors have limitations in achieving fully independent trait control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence, with steering one trait inducing changes in others.
Enforcing geometric independence through hard orthonormalisation does not eliminate cross-trait effects and reduces fluency.
Cross-trait dependencies are consistent across different model families like LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B.
Model-specific modulation exists, e.g., Neuroticism steering is strong in LLaMA-3 but weak in Mistral-8B.
Soft constraint methods like selective or soft projection offer a better trade-off between disentanglement and semantic preservation.
papers.limitation:
Limited to a small set of large language models and personality datasets.
Relies on linear geometric constraints; other orthogonalisation or projection methods are not explored.
Uses LLMs as judges for behavioral assessment without human evaluation.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a broader range of model families and trait representations.
Explore other orthogonalisation or projection methods beyond linear constraints.
Incorporate human evaluation or complementary metrics for assessment.
papers.abstract: Personality steering in large language models (LLMs) commonly relies on injecting trait-specific steering vectors, implicitly assuming that personality traits can be controlled independently. In this work, we examine whether this assumption holds by analysing the geometric relationships between Big Five personality steering directions. We study steering vectors extracted from two model families (LLaMA-3-8B and Mistral-8B) and apply a range of geometric conditioning schemes, from unconstrained directions to soft and hard orthonormalisation. Our results show that personality steering directions exhibit substantial geometric dependence: steering one trait consistently induces changes in others, even when linear overlap is explicitly removed. While hard orthonormalisation enforces geometric independence, it does not eliminate cross-trait behavioural effects and can reduce steering strength. These findings suggest that personality traits in LLMs occupy a slightly coupled subspace, limiting fully independent trait control.

papers.title: The Hypocrisy Gap: Quantifying Divergence Between Internal Belief and Chain-of-Thought Explanation via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the divergence between a model's internal belief and its chain-of-thought explanation to detect unfaithful behavior like sycophancy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric using Sparse Autoencoders to quantify divergence between a model's internal truth alignment and its chain-of-thought explanation, and demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting sycophantic behavior.
papers.conclusion: The Hypocrisy Gap provides a practical white-box diagnostic for unfaithful rationalizations in LLMs, highlighting a concrete latent signature of when models say what they do not believe.
papers.key_findings:
The Hypocrisy Gap achieves AUROC of 0.55–0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55–0.74 for hypocritical cases, outperforming a log-probability baseline (0.41–0.50 AUROC).
Sycophantic runs concentrate in a specific quadrant where internal truth scores are high but explanation truth scores are low, indicating unfaithful rationalization.
The method is lightweight, requiring only cached activations, a pretrained SAE encoder, and a sparse linear probe.
Task-specific SAE training and fine-tuning can improve performance but require additional compute and data.
The neutral truth score (T) alone provides modest signal for sycophancy detection, while the explanation score (F) is a poor indicator.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to internal activations and a compatible pretrained SAE, so it does not apply to closed-weight or API-based models.
The learned truth direction may capture template-, model-, or layer-specific correlations rather than a template-invariant representation of factual correctness.
Averaging CoT activations over continuation tokens can blur distinct phases of reasoning; more granular temporal aggregation may yield sharper signals.
Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark and a limited set of models, so generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings remains uncertain.
The metric operationalizes 'internal belief' as alignment with a learned truth direction in representation space and should not be interpreted as an agentic or philosophical notion of belief.
future_direction: More granular temporal aggregation of CoT activations to yield sharper signals.
Generalization to other domains, alternative forms of deception, and multilingual settings.
More rigorous training of task-specific SAEs on more examples to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently exhibit unfaithful behavior, producing a final answer that differs significantly from their internal chain of thought (CoT) reasoning in order to appease the user they are conversing with. In order to better detect this behavior, we introduce the Hypocrisy Gap, a mechanistic metric utilizing Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to quantify the divergence between a model's internal reasoning and its final generation. By mathematically comparing an internal truth belief, derived via sparse linear probes, to the final generated trajectory in latent space, we quantify and detect a model's tendency to engage in unfaithful behavior. Experiments on Gemma, Llama, and Qwen models using Anthropic's Sycophancy benchmark show that our method achieves an AUROC of 0.55-0.73 for detecting sycophantic runs and 0.55-0.74 for hypocritical cases where the model internally "knows" the user is wrong, consistently outperforming a decision-aligned log-probability baseline (0.41-0.50 AUROC).

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Linear representations in language models can change dramatically over a conversation
papers.research_question: How do linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models change over the course of a conversation?
papers.core_contribution: Linear representations of high-level concepts (e.g., factuality, ethics) in language models can change dramatically over the course of a conversation, flipping their meaning, which challenges static interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: Representational dynamics over conversations pose challenges for interpretability and safety (e.g., static probes may be misleading), but also point to new research directions for understanding contextual adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of factuality and ethics can flip over a conversation (e.g., in opposite day prompt).
These changes are content-dependent: generic information is preserved, while conversation-relevant information flips.
Changes occur across different model families and layers of the model.
Changes happen even when replaying off-policy conversations (scripts from other models).
Larger models show more dramatic representational changes.
papers.limitation: Evaluated a relatively small set of conversations due to the need to tailor question sets to each conversation.
future_direction: Understanding how models' representations change in various applications (e.g., codebases).
Developing more robust interpretability and safety methods that account for representation dynamics.
Methods to control adaptability (increase or decrease) for safety.
papers.abstract: Language model representations often contain linear directions that correspond to high-level concepts. Here, we study the dynamics of these representations: how representations evolve along these dimensions within the context of (simulated) conversations. We find that linear representations can change dramatically over a conversation; for example, information that is represented as factual at the beginning of a conversation can be represented as non-factual at the end and vice versa. These changes are content-dependent; while representations of conversation-relevant information may change, generic information is generally preserved. These changes are robust even for dimensions that disentangle factuality from more superficial response patterns, and occur across different model families and layers of the model. These representation changes do not require on-policy conversations; even replaying a conversation script written by an entirely different model can produce similar changes. However, adaptation is much weaker from simply having a sci-fi story in context that is framed more explicitly as such. We also show that steering along a representational direction can have dramatically different effects at different points in a conversation. These results are consistent with the idea that representations may evolve in response to the model playing a particular role that is cued by a conversation. Our findings may pose challenges for interpretability and steering -- in particular, they imply that it may be misleading to use static interpretations of features or directions, or probes that assume a particular range of features consistently corresponds to a particular ground-truth value. However, these types of representational dynamics also point to exciting new research directions for understanding how models adapt to context.

papers.title: Anchors in the Machine: Behavioral and Attributional Evidence of Anchoring Bias in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does anchoring bias in LLMs reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts in internal mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Integrates log-probability-based behavioral analysis with exact Shapley-value attribution to measure anchoring bias in LLMs, introducing an Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score.
papers.conclusion: Anchoring bias in LLMs is robust and quantifiable, with implications for using LLMs as decision systems and for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Robust anchoring effects are observed in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution showing that anchors influence reweighting.
Smaller models like GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability in anchoring sensitivity, suggesting scale may modulate effects.
Attributional effects vary across prompt designs, indicating fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes.
The Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score (ABSS) ranks models based on combined behavioral and attributional evidence.
Behavioral anchoring is consistent across models, but attribution alignment can be discordant, especially in smaller models.
papers.limitation:
Discretization of outputs to fixed numeric strings
No mechanistic claims as internal parameters and circuits were not probed
Method only works for models with open log-probabilities of outputs
future_direction: Expanding to a broader set of models
Integrating attributional evidence with concept-based and mechanistic interpretability
Extending the methodology to other cognitive biases
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly examined as both behavioral subjects and decision systems, yet it remains unclear whether observed cognitive biases reflect surface imitation or deeper probability shifts. Anchoring bias, a classic human judgment bias, offers a critical test case. While prior work shows LLMs exhibit anchoring, most evidence relies on surface-level outputs, leaving internal mechanisms and attributional contributions unexplored. This paper advances the study of anchoring in LLMs through three contributions: (1) a log-probability-based behavioral analysis showing that anchors shift entire output distributions, with controls for training-data contamination; (2) exact Shapley-value attribution over structured prompt fields to quantify anchor influence on model log-probabilities; and (3) a unified Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score integrating behavioral and attributional evidence across six open-source models. Results reveal robust anchoring effects in Gemma-2B, Phi-2, and Llama-2-7B, with attribution signaling that the anchors influence reweighting. Smaller models such as GPT-2, Falcon-RW-1B, and GPT-Neo-125M show variability, suggesting scale may modulate sensitivity. Attributional effects, however, vary across prompt designs, underscoring fragility in treating LLMs as human substitutes. The findings demonstrate that anchoring bias in LLMs is robust, measurable, and interpretable, while highlighting risks in applied domains. More broadly, the framework bridges behavioral science, LLM safety, and interpretability, offering a reproducible path for evaluating other cognitive biases in LLMs.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: Interpretable Deep Learning for Enhanced AI Trust and Clarity
papers.research_question: How do interpretability tools like SHAP and LIME enhance user trust and transparency in deep learning models, particularly in high-risk applications?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that interpretability tools like SHAP and LIME significantly enhance user trust in AI systems, with SHAP excelling in global interpretability and LIME in local interpretability, and visualization aids comprehension for non-technical users.
papers.conclusion: Model interpretability significantly enhances user trust in AI systems; SHAP provides global interpretability, LIME provides case-specific understanding, and visualization tools improve comprehension, though SHAP has higher computational demands.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP provides strong global interpretability with feature importance scores, enhancing transparency in complex models like CNNs.
LIME offers effective localized explanations for individual predictions, useful for case-by-case interpretability.
Visualization tools like heatmaps significantly improve user understanding, especially for non-technical users.
Interpretability tools increase user trust, with SHAP showing higher trust scores than LIME.
Computational efficiency varies, with SHAP being more resource-intensive than LIME.
papers.limitation:
Computational efficiency challenges remain, especially with SHAP
LIME's explanations can vary across repeated runs, which some users found confusing
future_direction: Explore hybrid interpretability approaches
Develop adaptive user interfaces to improve accessibility and performance
papers.abstract: This research aims to explore the role of interpretability in increasing user trust in artificial intelligence (AI) systems through tools such as Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME). The study stands out with its approach of comparing the effectiveness of two popular interpretability techniques in bringing transparency to deep learning models, particularly in high-risk applications such as health and finance. The research method involves applying the interpretability tools to AI models and evaluating user confidence and perception of transparency using feature visualization. Results show that interpretability has been significant in increasing user confidence, with SHAP excelling in providing global interpretation and LIME providing clarity on specific predictions. Visualizations proved effective for nontechnical users in understanding model decisions, although computational efficiency challenges remain, especially with SHAP. In conclusion, interpretability supports the ethical use of AI by increasing accountability and accessibility, and it demonstrates the importance of selecting interpretability tools based on context and user needs. The results provide practical direction for AI developers in integrating interpretability from the design stage to ensure transparency and reliability.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: A simple probabilistic neural network for machine understanding
papers.research_question: What are the properties of learning machines with a fixed internal representation, derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, in unsupervised learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM), a probabilistic neural network with a fixed internal representation derived from principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance, and shows that it has desirable properties like continuity, controllable compression, and ability to support functions beyond generalization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that learning machines with a fixed internal representation, such as the HFM, operate in a qualitatively different regime from traditional models like RBMs, with data-specific information stored in weights and potential for higher cognitive functions.
papers.key_findings:
The HFM is uniquely identified by the principles of maximal relevance and maximal ignorance when hidden units are binary.
The HFM exhibits a phase transition at a critical coupling parameter g, with a divergence in specific heat.
Training the HFM with an EM algorithm allows features to be learned sequentially, with low-order features remaining stable as new features are added.
The internal representation of the HFM is robust to changes in the coupling parameter and dataset size, and low-order features capture most of the relevant information.
The learning modality of HFM is qualitatively different from RBMs: in HFM, data-specific information is stored in the weights, while in RBMs it is transferred to the internal representation.
future_direction: Investigating whether a universal data-independent internal representation emerges spontaneously in deep layers of learning architectures.
Relating the findings to thermodynamic costs of learning.
Exploring the hypothesis that internal representations evolve with depth in hierarchical learning systems.
papers.abstract: We discuss probabilistic neural networks with a fixed internal representation as models for machine understanding. Here understanding is intended as mapping data to an already existing representation which encodes an {\em a priori} organisation of the feature space. We derive the internal representation by requiring that it satisfies the principles of maximal relevance and of maximal ignorance about how different features are combined. We show that, when hidden units are binary variables, these two principles identify a unique model -- the Hierarchical Feature Model (HFM) -- which is fully solvable and provides a natural interpretation in terms of features. We argue that learning machines with this architecture enjoy a number of interesting properties, like the continuity of the representation with respect to changes in parameters and data, the possibility to control the level of compression and the ability to support functions that go beyond generalisation. We explore the behaviour of the model with extensive numerical experiments and argue that models where the internal representation is fixed reproduce a learning modality which is qualitatively different from that of traditional models such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines.

papers.title: LENS: Learning Ensemble Confidence from Neural States for Multi-LLM Answer Integration
papers.research_question: How can we effectively combine predictions from multiple LLMs by learning to estimate each model's context-dependent confidence from its internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LENS, a novel ensemble method that learns lightweight linear confidence predictors for each LLM using layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities, enabling more effective weighting of model predictions based on context-dependent reliability.
papers.conclusion: LENS is a simple yet effective ensemble method that leverages model confidence patterns learned from internal representations to improve performance across diverse question-answering tasks, offering a practical and scalable solution for robust LLM ensembles.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Max Confidence ensemble method outperforms baseline methods (Majority Vote and Probability Max) on 5 out of 6 evaluated datasets.
Internal representations (hidden states) contain valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.
The method is simple to implement, computationally efficient, and does not require retraining or modifying the base LLMs.
The approach generalizes well across diverse question-answering tasks, including logical reasoning, commonsense inference, and mathematics.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation is restricted to decoder-only transformer architectures, limiting applicability to encoder-decoder or other model types.
The method requires access to intermediate layer representations, which may not be available in production environments or with commercial API-based models.
future_direction: Investigating cross-task transferability of learned confidence patterns for zero-shot ensemble learning.
Extending the method to modern multi-LLM systems and agent collaboration scenarios.
Leveraging confidence patterns and intermediate representations to enhance understanding of LLM decision-making processes (model interpretability).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, with different models excelling in distinct domains and specific abilities. Effectively combining the predictions of multiple LLMs is crucial for enhancing system robustness and performance. However, existing ensemble methods often rely on simple techniques like voting or logits ensembling, which overlook the varying confidence and reliability of models in different contexts. In this work, we propose LENS (Learning ENsemble confidence from Neural States), a novel approach that learns to estimate model confidence by analyzing internal representations. For each LLM, we train a lightweight linear confidence predictor that leverages layer-wise hidden states and normalized probabilities as inputs. This allows for more nuanced weighting of model predictions based on their context-dependent reliability. Our method does not require modifying the model parameters and requires negligible additional computation. Experimental results on multiple-choice and boolean question-answering tasks demonstrate that LENS outperforms traditional ensemble methods by a substantial margin. Our findings suggest that internal representations provide valuable signals for determining model confidence and can be effectively leveraged for ensemble learning.

papers.title: On the Effect of Uncertainty on Layer-wise Inference Dynamics
papers.research_question: How does uncertainty affect the inference dynamics of models, and does model competence affect the ability to adapt inference dynamics to uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that uncertainty does not significantly affect the inference dynamics of LLMs, as probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are aligned. It also provides preliminary evidence that more competent models may exhibit adaptive inference dynamics.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit similar token probability dynamics and tend to commit to final decisions at specific layers largely independent of output uncertainty, but show potential for greater adaptability in inference dynamics as model competence increases.
papers.key_findings:
Probability trajectories for correct and incorrect predictions are strongly aligned across layers, with abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers.
Prediction depth distributions are similar for correct and incorrect answers, indicating the model commits to its output at similar layers regardless of uncertainty.
Weak but consistent positive correlations exist between answer incorrectness and prediction depth across models and datasets.
Positive correlation between task proficiency (measured by Cohen's Kappa) and prediction depth difference suggests adaptive inference dynamics may emerge with greater model competence.
The findings challenge the feasibility of using simplistic methods for uncertainty detection at inference and suggest more nuanced interpretability approaches are needed.
papers.limitation:
The study is exploratory and requires further validation on more models, especially more competent ones.
More rigorous tests are needed, including analyses with varying levels of uncertainty and accounting for hallucination on known knowledge.
future_direction: Further testing on more models to validate the results, especially on more competent models.
More rigorous tests that include analyses using varying levels of uncertainty and accounts for hallucination on known knowledge.
Similar experiments for aleatoric uncertainty for a more thorough investigation.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) internally represent and process their predictions is central to detecting uncertainty and preventing hallucinations. While several studies have shown that models encode uncertainty in their hidden states, it is underexplored how this affects the way they process such hidden states. In this work, we demonstrate that the dynamics of output token probabilities across layers for certain and uncertain outputs are largely aligned, revealing that uncertainty does not seem to affect inference dynamics. Specifically, we use the Tuned Lens, a variant of the Logit Lens, to analyze the layer-wise probability trajectories of final prediction tokens across 11 datasets and 5 models. Using incorrect predictions as those with higher epistemic uncertainty, our results show aligned trajectories for certain and uncertain predictions that both observe abrupt increases in confidence at similar layers. We balance this finding by showing evidence that more competent models may learn to process uncertainty differently. Our findings challenge the feasibility of leveraging simplistic methods for detecting uncertainty at inference. More broadly, our work demonstrates how interpretability methods may be used to investigate the way uncertainty affects inference.

papers.title: Decomposing Theory of Mind: How Emotional Processing Mediates ToM Abilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: What cognitive processes change in LLMs when activation steering improves Theory of Mind performance, and how does emotional processing mediate these abilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that improved Theory of Mind performance in LLMs via activation steering is mediated by increased emotional processing and decreased analytical processes, suggesting emotional understanding is key to perspective-taking.
papers.conclusion: Steering improves ToM by enhancing emotional and generative processes while inhibiting analytical ones, offering a new mechanistic understanding of perspective-taking in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering improves ToM accuracy on belief attribution tasks by 14.2% (from 32.5% to 46.7%).
Emotional processes (e.g., emotion perception, emotion valuing) are amplified during successful perspective-taking.
Analytical processes (e.g., questioning, convergent thinking) are suppressed during successful perspective-taking.
Cognitive action probes can effectively decompose and analyze steering effects on internal processes.
Successful perspective-taking in LLMs is mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.
papers.limitation: Findings may not generalize to human cognition, and the methodology does not validate such comparisons.
future_direction: Validate findings with multiple, bigger models and additional data sources.
papers.abstract: Recent work shows activation steering substantially improves language models' Theory of Mind (ToM) (Bortoletto et al. 2024), yet the mechanisms of what changes occur internally that leads to different outputs remains unclear. We propose decomposing ToM in LLMs by comparing steered versus baseline LLMs' activations using linear probes trained on 45 cognitive actions. We applied Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering to Gemma-3-4B and evaluated it on 1,000 BigToM forward belief scenarios (Gandhi et al. 2023), we find improved performance on belief attribution tasks (32.5\% to 46.7\% accuracy) is mediated by activations processing emotional content : emotion perception (+2.23), emotion valuing (+2.20), while suppressing analytical processes: questioning (-0.78), convergent thinking (-1.59). This suggests that successful ToM abilities in LLMs are mediated by emotional understanding, not analytical reasoning.

papers.title: Explainable Verbal Deception Detection using Transformers
papers.research_question: How can transformer-based models improve automated verbal deception detection, and how can these models be interpreted to understand the linguistic mechanisms involved in deception?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes and evaluates several transformer-based models for verbal deception detection, showing they outperform traditional machine learning and human baselines, and uses LIME and linguistic analysis to interpret the models and understand differences between truthful and deceptive statements.
papers.conclusion: Transformer-based models enhance automated deception detection performance, and explainability techniques like LIME, combined with linguistic analysis, help understand how these models classify statements and reveal linguistic differences between truthful and deceptive texts.
papers.key_findings:
The BERT+Co-Attention model achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 70.61% and F1-score of 73.33%, outperforming the previous best baseline by +2.11% in accuracy.
Using both statements (Q1 and Q2) concurrently improves classification performance compared to using a single statement.
Truthful and deceptive statements show significant differences in vocabulary (low Jaccard index) and in the usage of specific LIWC categories (e.g., truthful statements correlate with ingestion, biological processes, analytical thinking; deceptive statements with apostrophes, past focus, personal pronouns).
LIME analysis indicates that misclassifications often occur when statements contain LIWC categories strongly correlated with the opposite class.
The study demonstrates that advanced deep learning models can be used for deception detection without sacrificing explainability through post-hoc interpretation methods.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameter tuning was not performed, which could lead to higher evaluation results if done.
Misclassifications occur when truthful statements contain words significantly correlated with deceptive statements and vice versa, indicating the model may need more contextualized information.
LIME is a post-hoc explanation method, and the surrogate models it learns may rely on different mechanisms than the original model, raising fidelity concerns.
Training on two datasets increased training time and GPU resource usage.
future_direction: Expand the approach to other datasets and domains and examine other transformer-based models (e.g., ALBERT, XLNet).
Use interpretable (self-explaining) models to mitigate the limitations of post-hoc methods like LIME.
Adopt continual learning methods to save time and resources while maintaining or improving performance across datasets.
papers.abstract: People are regularly confronted with potentially deceptive statements (e.g., fake news, misleading product reviews, or lies about activities). Only few works on automated text-based deception detection have exploited the potential of deep learning approaches. A critique of deep-learning methods is their lack of interpretability, preventing us from understanding the underlying (linguistic) mechanisms involved in deception. However, recent advancements have made it possible to explain some aspects of such models. This paper proposes and evaluates six deep-learning models, including combinations of BERT (and RoBERTa), MultiHead Attention, co-attentions, and transformers. To understand how the models reach their decisions, we then examine the model's predictions with LIME. We then zoom in on vocabulary uniqueness and the correlation of LIWC categories with the outcome class (truthful vs deceptive). The findings suggest that our transformer-based models can enhance automated deception detection performances (+2.11% in accuracy) and show significant differences pertinent to the usage of LIWC features in truthful and deceptive statements.

papers.title: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception
papers.research_question: How can we elicit, measure, and detect open-ended, long-term agentic deception in LLM-agents using a sandbox environment?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Among Us sandbox and Deception Elo metric to study open-ended agentic deception, and shows that frontier models are better at deception than detection, while linear probes can detect deception out-of-distribution.
papers.conclusion: The Among Us sandbox and Deception Elo metric provide a valuable environment for studying agentic deception, and interpretability techniques like linear probes are effective for out-of-distribution deception detection, contributing to AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Frontier reasoning models are differentially better at producing deception than at detecting it.
Linear probes trained on dishonesty datasets (e.g., RepEng, DishonestQA) generalize extremely well to detect deception in the Among Us sandbox, achieving AUROCs over 95%.
Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features can detect deception out-of-distribution but are ineffective for steering models to lie less.
The Among Us sandbox successfully elicits open-ended, long-term deceptive behavior from LLM-agents without fine-tuning or in-context examples.
Models trained with reinforcement learning (RL) are comparatively much better at producing deception than detecting it.
papers.limitation:
The results might not represent real-world user-model interaction, or the deception mechanisms in the sandbox could differ from real-world settings.
The techniques might work for uninteresting reasons (e.g., detecting impostor/crewmate tokens based on latent knowledge associations).
Potential failure mode of sandbagging, where models strategically underperform.
Models likely have prior knowledge of Among Us from pre-training, which may influence behavior.
future_direction: Conduct more experiments with different models and safety techniques, including responsible human trials.
Train models for deception in the controlled sandbox to study generalization and superhuman capabilities.
Explore other model organisms and sandboxes for studying deception, including more real-world scenarios and games that decouple deception from fixed role assignment.
papers.abstract: Prior studies on deception in language-based AI agents typically assess whether the agent produces a false statement about a topic, or makes a binary choice prompted by a goal, rather than allowing open-ended deceptive behavior to emerge in pursuit of a longer-term goal. To fix this, we introduce Among Us, a sandbox social deception game where LLM-agents exhibit long-term, open-ended deception as a consequence of the game objectives. While most benchmarks saturate quickly, Among Us can be expected to last much longer, because it is a multi-player game far from equilibrium. Using the sandbox, we evaluate 18 proprietary and open-weight LLMs and uncover a general trend: models trained with RL are comparatively much better at producing deception than detecting it. We evaluate the effectiveness of methods to detect lying and deception: logistic regression on the activations and sparse autoencoders (SAEs). We find that probes trained on a dataset of "pretend you're a dishonest model:.." generalize extremely well out-of-distribution, consistently obtaining AUROCs over 95% even when evaluated just on the deceptive statement, without the chain of thought. We also find two SAE features that work well at deception detection but are unable to steer the model to lie less. We hope our open-sourced sandbox, game logs, and probes serve to anticipate and mitigate deceptive behavior and capabilities in language-based agents.

papers.title: Explanations of Large Language Models Explain Language Representations in the Brain
papers.research_question: Are LLM-derived explanations effective in explaining language processing in the brain? Do the observed similarities between LLMs and the brain arise from shared pathways or are they simply artifacts of high-dimensional feature spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Attribution methods from explainable AI (XAI) can robustly predict brain activity during language processing, revealing a hierarchical alignment where early model layers correspond to early brain processing stages and later layers to higher-order stages.
