papers.conclusion: XAI methods, particularly attribution, provide a powerful tool for linking LLMs and the brain, revealing shared computational principles for language processing and offering a brain-alignment framework for assessing explanation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution methods (Gradient Norm and Gradient × Input) predict brain activity across the language network, outperforming internal representations (activations, attention) in early language processing regions.
A hierarchical alignment exists: explanations from early LLM layers align with early brain processing areas (e.g., auditory cortex), while later layers align with higher-order areas (e.g., inferior frontal gyrus).
Layers with greater influence on next-word prediction (higher attribution scores) show stronger brain alignment, with a strong correlation between layer importance for prediction and brain alignment.
The predictive capability of attribution methods is consistent across participants and stories, and they encode brain-relevant information in a more compact representation compared to high-dimensional internal representations.
The study positions attribution methods as a powerful tool for bridging LLMs and the brain, offering a novel framework for evaluating XAI methods via neurobiological alignment.
future_direction: Examining a broader range of models, attribution techniques, and brain recording modalities to identify factors shaping alignment.
Extending the brain-explanation alignment approach to other cognitive domains (vision, auditory perception) and multimodal models.
Quantitatively comparing brain-based evaluation frameworks with traditional behavioral evaluation methods for XAI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) not only exhibit human-like performance but also share computational principles with the brain's language processing mechanisms. While prior research has focused on mapping LLMs' internal representations to neural activity, we propose a novel approach using explainable AI (XAI) to strengthen this link. Applying attribution methods, we quantify the influence of preceding words on LLMs' next-word predictions and use these explanations to predict fMRI data from participants listening to narratives. We find that attribution methods robustly predict brain activity across the language network, revealing a hierarchical pattern: explanations from early layers align with the brain's initial language processing stages, while later layers correspond to more advanced stages. Additionally, layers with greater influence on next-word prediction$\unicode{x2014}$reflected in higher attribution scores$\unicode{x2014}$demonstrate stronger brain alignment. These results underscore XAI's potential for exploring the neural basis of language and suggest brain alignment for assessing the biological plausibility of explanation methods.

papers.title: Explainable AI for cyber threat Intelligence: Enhancing analyst trust
papers.research_question: How can Explainable AI (XAI) techniques improve analyst trust and decision-making in cyber threat intelligence systems?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that integrating Explainable AI (XAI) techniques like SHAP and LIME into cyber threat intelligence systems enhances analyst trust, reduces investigation time, and improves threat detection accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The integration of Explainable AI (XAI) into Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) systems represents a significant advancement in trust, transparency, and operational effectiveness, improving threat comprehension, reducing time-to-response, and fostering collaboration between human analysts and AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Integration of XAI techniques improved detection accuracy by 2.7% and reduced false positive rate by over 50%.
Analyst response time decreased by 31.5% when using XAI explanations.
Analyst trust scores increased by 45.8% with XAI-integrated systems.
XAI explanations, particularly SHAP and LIME, enhanced analyst comprehension and decision-making speed.
The study found that XAI fosters collaborative human-AI interaction in cybersecurity operations.
papers.limitation:
The experiment was limited to a synthetic environment and a single dataset.
Computational cost of XAI techniques like SHAP may not scale well in real-time environments.
Not all explanations were equally useful; effectiveness depends on user cognitive style and task context.
future_direction: Scalability and real-time constraints for XAI in high-speed SOC environments
Explainability in cyber-physical systems with hybrid XAI models
XAI for IoT and federated learning-based threat detection
papers.abstract: With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) in the ecosystem of contemporary cyber threat intelligence (CTI) platforms, the issue of AI-driven decision interpretability and transparency has become increasingly common. Although there is an increased ability in machine learning models to detect the complex and evolving cyber threats, this usually prevents human trust and restricts perceived actionable insights because they are black boxed and have a challenge of accountability. This paper discusses the use of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI, including SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), LIME (Local interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations), and attention-based visualizations, in order to achieve better interpretability in CTI systems. We provide a case study illustrating that incorporation of XAI to threat detection pipelines enhances the analysis comprehension by analysts, saves investigation time, and enables informed decision-making within Security Operations Centers (SOCs). The evidence provided by our research indicates that XAI does not only make complex AI models understandable to human analysts yet can create a collaborative and transparent cybersecurity ecosystem. The study offers a viable system to implement XAI-enriched CTI that would enable more responsible and successful AI-empowered cybersecurity.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: Emergent Moral Representations in Large Language Models Aligns with Human Conceptual, Neural, and Behavioral Moral Structure
papers.research_question: Do large language models internally encode structured representations of morality that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models spontaneously develop dissociable and structured moral representations whose internal geometry parallels human neural and behavioral moral structures, positioning them as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs acquire moral representations that parallel human moral cognition, suggesting they can serve as computational models for moral reasoning and value alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations of LLMs, with peak discriminability in mid layers.
The representational geometry of moral foundations in LLMs aligns with human conceptual taxonomies (e.g., Individualizing vs. Binding/Social, Moral vs. Social).
LLM mid-layer activations predict human wrongness judgments.
The posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) in humans shows robust decoding of moral foundations and its representational structure aligns with LLM mid-layer activations.
Partial least squares correlation reveals orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and higher-order abstractions.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in ethically sensitive settings, yet it remains unclear whether they internally encode structured representations of morality. Here we examine the activation space representations of several mid-sized LLMs to test whether statistical learning over text gives rise to moral distinctions that parallel human conceptual, behavioral, and neural organization. Using multivariate decoding, representational similarity analysis, partial least squares correlation, and behavioral prediction, we show that moral foundations are linearly decodable from hidden activations, with peak discriminability in mid layers. Representational similarity analysis uncovered a hierarchical moral geometry consistent with Moral Foundations Theory, with the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) showing robust multivariate decoding and a representational structure that aligned most strongly with mid-layer LLM activations. These same mid-layers also predicted human wrongness judgments, indicating a shared computational substrate for moral evaluation. Partial least squares correlation further revealed orthogonal activation dimensions corresponding to individual foundations and their higher-order abstractions, yielding interpretable axes along which moral meaning is encoded. These results reveal a striking convergence across conceptual, behavioral, neural, and model representations, positioning LLMs as emerging neurocognitive models of moral reasoning and offering a window into the internal mechanisms that shape their behavior in sensitive domains. Such alignment may enable more explainable and transparent AI systems and support future efforts to ground LLMs in human values.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: Revealing the Parametric Knowledge of Language Models: A Unified Framework for Attribution Methods
papers.research_question: What are the differences and complementary insights between instance attribution and neuron attribution methods in revealing the parametric knowledge of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified evaluation framework to compare instance and neuron attribution methods, showing that NA reveals more diverse knowledge while IA provides unique insights, suggesting a synergistic approach for holistic understanding.
papers.conclusion: IA and NA provide different explanations for parametric knowledge, suggesting a combined approach for holistic understanding. Neurons in MLP layers are insufficient, indicating attention weights also play a crucial role.
papers.key_findings:
NA-Instances discovers more diverse training instances than IA methods.
Neurons in MLP layers are not sufficient nor comprehensive for explaining predictions, indicating importance of attention layers.
Fine-tuning with influential instances from IA does not outperform random selection.
NA-Instances performs better at discovering dataset artifacts than IA methods.
IA and NA results have small overlap, suggesting complementary insights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments limited to two instance attribution methods, one neuron attribution method, three tasks, three language models, and English text only.
Computational restrictions prevented studying very large language models.
Only neurons in MLP layers were studied, not attention heads, so the interplay between MLP and attention is not captured.
future_direction: Investigate other NLP tasks and more language models, including very large ones and cross-lingual scenarios.
Study the interplay between MLP neurons and attention heads for a more complete understanding.
Further study the purpose of attribution methods, e.g., for dataset artifact detection.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) acquire parametric knowledge from their training process, embedding it within their weights. The increasing scalability of LMs, however, poses significant challenges for understanding a model's inner workings and further for updating or correcting this embedded knowledge without the significant cost of retraining. This underscores the importance of unveiling exactly what knowledge is stored and its association with specific model components. Instance Attribution (IA) and Neuron Attribution (NA) offer insights into this training-acquired knowledge, though they have not been compared systematically. Our study introduces a novel evaluation framework to quantify and compare the knowledge revealed by IA and NA. To align the results of the methods we introduce the attribution method NA-Instances to apply NA for retrieving influential training instances, and IA-Neurons to discover important neurons of influential instances discovered by IA. We further propose a comprehensive list of faithfulness tests to evaluate the comprehensiveness and sufficiency of the explanations provided by both methods. Through extensive experiments and analysis, we demonstrate that NA generally reveals more diverse and comprehensive information regarding the LM's parametric knowledge compared to IA. Nevertheless, IA provides unique and valuable insights into the LM's parametric knowledge, which are not revealed by NA. Our findings further suggest the potential of a synergistic approach of combining the diverse findings of IA and NA for a more holistic understanding of an LM's parametric knowledge.

papers.title: Minimal and Mechanistic Conditions for Behavioral Self-Awareness in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the minimal and mechanistic conditions under which behavioral self-awareness emerges in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs can be induced with a single rank-1 LoRA adapter, captured by a single steering vector in activation space, and is domain-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Behavioral self-awareness in LLMs emerges as a linear, domain-localized feature that can be easily induced and modulated, raising security concerns but providing interpretability insights.
papers.key_findings:
Self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter on a single layer.
The learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect.
Self-awareness representations are non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks.
Steering vectors derived from PCA or gradient-based optimization can effectively induce self-aware behavior.
Cross-domain transfer of steering vectors shows minimal effect, supporting domain isolation.
papers.limitation: A small performance gap remains between rank-1 LoRA and full-layer fine-tuning in the Make Me Say tasks due to greater behavioral and linguistic complexity.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed that LLMs can exhibit behavioral self-awareness: the ability to accurately describe or predict their own learned behaviors without explicit supervision. This capability raises safety concerns as it may, for example, allow models to better conceal their true abilities during evaluation. We attempt to characterize the minimal conditions under which such self-awareness emerges, and the mechanistic processes through which it manifests. Through controlled finetuning experiments on instruction-tuned LLMs with low-rank adapters (LoRA), we find: (1) that self-awareness can be reliably induced using a single rank-1 LoRA adapter; (2) that the learned self-aware behavior can be largely captured by a single steering vector in activation space, recovering nearly all of the fine-tune's behavioral effect; and (3) that self-awareness is non-universal and domain-localized, with independent representations across tasks. Together, these findings suggest that behavioral self-awareness emerges as a domain-specific, linear feature that can be easily induced and modulated.

papers.title: Enhancing Transparency and Trust in Brain Tumor Diagnosis: An In-Depth Analysis of Deep Learning and Explainable AI Techniques
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI techniques improve transparency and trust in brain tumor diagnosis using deep learning and machine learning methods?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of deep learning and explainable AI techniques in brain tumor diagnosis, highlighting strengths, limitations, and future directions to enhance transparency and clinical trust.
papers.conclusion: Explainable AI techniques improve transparency in brain tumor diagnosis, but issues like generalizability and computational complexity must be addressed to fully realize their clinical potential.
papers.key_findings:
XAI techniques like Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME enhance model interpretability in brain tumor diagnosis.
Challenges include generalizability, computational complexity, and dataset quality.
CNNs and Vision Transformers are commonly used with high accuracy.
Open-source code availability is limited, affecting reproducibility.
Future research should address limitations in dataset diversity and model explainability.
future_direction: Addressing generalizability and computational complexity of XAI techniques
Improving dataset quality and diversity
Enhancing model transparency for clinical trust
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Brain tumors pose significant health risks due to their high mortality rates and challenges in early diagnosis. Advances in medical imaging, particularly MRI, combined with artificial intelligence (AI), have revolutionized tumor detection, segmentation, and classification. Despite the high accuracy of models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs), their clinical adoption is hampered by a lack of interpretability. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of machine learning, deep learning, and explainable AI (XAI) techniques in brain tumor diagnosis, emphasizing their strengths, limitations, and potential to improve transparency and clinical trust. By reviewing 53 peer-reviewed articles published between 2017 and 2024, we assess the current state of research, identify gaps, and provide practical recommendations for clinicians, regulators, and AI developers. The findings reveal that while XAI techniques, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, and LIME, significantly enhance model interpretability, challenges remain in terms of generalizability, computational complexity, and dataset quality. Future research should focus on addressing these limitations to fully realize the potential of AI in brain tumor diagnostics.

papers.title: Calibration Meets Explanation: A Simple and Effective Approach for Model Confidence Estimates
papers.research_question: Can model explanations help confidence calibration? If so, how should we exploit the predictive power of these explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method (CME) that leverages model explanations (token attributions) during training to improve the calibration of confidence estimates in pre-trained language models.
papers.conclusion: Model explanations can be leveraged to calibrate the confidence estimates of black-box models, and the proposed CME method effectively reduces calibration errors.
papers.key_findings:
CME achieves the lowest expected calibration errors (ECEs) in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings without accuracy drops.
CME is complementary to post-hoc calibration techniques like temperature scaling, further reducing ECEs when combined.
The method is effective across different tasks (natural language inference, paraphrase detection, commonsense reasoning) and model architectures (BERT, RoBERTa).
Label smoothing (LS) can sometimes harm calibration, but CME+LS can still improve calibration in some out-of-domain settings.
Visualizations show CME helps calibrate confidence for cases near the decision boundary.
papers.limitation: The method is limited by the reliability and fidelity of the interpretable methods used to generate attributions.
future_direction: Explore using free-text explanations to help calibrate the model.
papers.abstract: Calibration strengthens the trustworthiness of black-box models by producing better accurate confidence estimates on given examples. However, little is known about if model explanations can help confidence calibration. Intuitively, humans look at important features attributions and decide whether the model is trustworthy. Similarly, the explanations can tell us when the model may or may not know. Inspired by this, we propose a method named CME that leverages model explanations to make the model less confident with non-inductive attributions. The idea is that when the model is not highly confident, it is difficult to identify strong indications of any class, and the tokens accordingly do not have high attribution scores for any class and vice versa. We conduct extensive experiments on six datasets with two popular pre-trained language models in the in-domain and out-of-domain settings. The results show that CME improves calibration performance in all settings. The expected calibration errors are further reduced when combined with temperature scaling. Our findings highlight that model explanations can help calibrate posterior estimates.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of internal representations in multilayer neural networks with binary weights
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the weight space structure of multilayer neural networks with binary weights, focusing on the distribution of volumes associated with internal representations of learning examples. It also analyzes the learning behavior and symmetry breaking transition in such networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies the internal representation volumes approach to multilayer neural networks with binary weights, deriving the distribution of volumes and analyzing learning behavior and symmetry breaking transitions, with numerical validation.
papers.conclusion: The internal representation volumes approach is confirmed by numerical simulations for binary weight networks, revealing differences from continuous weight networks in where symmetry breaking occurs.
papers.key_findings:
The distribution of internal representation volumes for the binary parity machine can be computed analytically, revealing a freezing transition at α=0.41.
The number of implementable internal representations NR and the number of domains contributing to the Gardner volume ND are derived as functions of the loading parameter α.
The analytical predictions show remarkable agreement with numerical simulations on finite systems.
Multilayer networks with binary weights exhibit symmetry breaking inside representation volumes, unlike continuous weights where it occurs between volumes.
The method provides a detailed geometrical interpretation of the learning transition and the freezing phenomena.
future_direction: Study of the distribution of metastable states arising from a gradient learning process.
papers.abstract: We study the weight space structure of the parity machine with binary weights by deriving the distribution of volumes associated to the internal representations of the learning examples. The learning behavior and the symmetry breaking transition are analyzed and the results are found to be in very good agreement with the extended numerical simulations. \textcopyright{} 1996 The American Physical Society.

papers.title: A Neural Network Model of Continual Learning with Cognitive Control
papers.research_question: How can cognitive control mechanisms mitigate catastrophic forgetting in neural networks during continual learning, and why might blocking trials be advantageous due to active maintenance biases?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks equipped with cognitive control mechanisms do not exhibit catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked, and show an advantage of blocking over interleaving when there is a bias for active maintenance in the control signal.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates computational principles that may underlie human continual learning and help explain behavioral phenomena observed in human experiments.
papers.key_findings:
The base MLP model exhibits catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked, but not when interleaved.
Adding a PFC gating mechanism alleviates catastrophic forgetting in the blocked condition.
With active maintenance bias in the control signal, blocking leads to better performance than interleaving due to switch costs.
There is a tradeoff between control strength and switch cost: stronger control reduces forgetting but increases switch cost.
Representational analysis shows that control modulates hidden representations by compressing irrelevant dimensions.
papers.limitation: The model's active maintenance may not be necessary for the task, and its absolute superiority over systems without such mechanisms is not proven.
future_direction: Introduce learning into the PFC module.
Investigate effects of active maintenance in more realistic implementations.
Assess dependence of results on initialization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks struggle in continual learning settings from catastrophic forgetting: when trials are blocked, new learning can overwrite the learning from previous blocks. Humans learn effectively in these settings, in some cases even showing an advantage of blocking, suggesting the brain contains mechanisms to overcome this problem. Here, we build on previous work and show that neural networks equipped with a mechanism for cognitive control do not exhibit catastrophic forgetting when trials are blocked. We further show an advantage of blocking over interleaving when there is a bias for active maintenance in the control signal, implying a tradeoff between maintenance and the strength of control. Analyses of map-like representations learned by the networks provided additional insights into these mechanisms. Our work highlights the potential of cognitive control to aid continual learning in neural networks, and offers an explanation for the advantage of blocking that has been observed in humans.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Analyzing the Hidden Activations of Deep Policy Networks: Why Representation Matters
papers.research_question: Is it possible to know a priori if a state representation will lead to fast learning in deep reinforcement learning agents, and how do neural network policies organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-learned latent representations accelerate policy learning by providing an innately organized internal representation, and a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for good policy learning.
papers.conclusion: Learning a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for effective policy learning, and using pre-learned latent representations can remove this burden, leading to accelerated training.
papers.key_findings:
Agents trained on latent representations learn significantly faster than those trained on raw pixel images.
The internal representation of policies using latent codes is organized around task rewards even before training begins.
A poor initial representation (e.g., raw pixels in a complex task) can cause an unrecoverable collapse in the policy network's internal representation.
The organization of the internal representation evolves during training and correlates with learning progress.
The innate organization provided by latent representations is robust to different weight initialization schemes.
papers.abstract: We analyze the hidden activations of neural network policies of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents and show, empirically, that it's possible to know a priori if a state representation will lend itself to fast learning. RL agents in high-dimensional states have two main learning burdens: (1) to learn an action-selection policy and (2) to learn to discern between useful and non-useful information in a given state. By learning a latent representation of these high-dimensional states with an auxiliary model, the latter burden is effectively removed, thereby leading to accelerated training progress. We examine this phenomenon across tasks in the PyBullet Kuka environment, where an agent must learn to control a robotic gripper to pick up an object. Our analysis reveals how neural network policies learn to organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training. The results from this analysis provide three main insights into how deep RL agents learn. First, a well-organized internal representation within the policy network is a prerequisite to learning good action-selection. Second, a poor initial representation can cause an unrecoverable collapse within a policy network. Third, a good initial representation allows an agent's policy network to organize its internal representation even before any training begins.

papers.title: Mechanistic Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we control large language models by understanding their inner working mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of language models can be leveraged to control their behavior in various applications, such as reducing hallucination, improving instruction stability, and enhancing planning in dialogues.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation shows that mechanistic control is a promising approach for aligning language models, and future work should expand the scope of interpretability and control to more complex behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns an emergent world representation of the Othello board, and this representation can be intervened on to edit the model's perceived world state.
Inference-time intervention (ITI) can elicit more truthful answers from language models by shifting activations along truthful directions found in attention heads.
Instruction drift in long conversations is caused by attention decay, and split-softmax can mitigate this drift by forcing the model to pay more attention to the system prompt.
Dialogue action tokens (DAT) enable better planning in multi-turn dialogues by using a planner to predict action vectors that steer the language model towards long-horizon goals.
papers.abstract: This dissertation talks about mechanistic control of large language models (LLM). The intuition is that, in order to rigorously control large language models, it is beneficial to first understand their inner working mechanisms. Even though a fully mechanistic understanding of language models is far from complete at the time this dissertation is written, I will demonstrate several cases where such understanding provides a useful surface for control. I argue that connecting interpretability to real-life applications--e.g., alignment and safety--offers advantages to the development of both fields. I first position this methodological approach within a broader scientific context, discussing and systematizing the role of interpretability in artificial intelligence research. I then present four intensive case studies, each leveraging certain interpretability insights to control the behavior of language models. The interpretability insights I explored span emergent world representations, representation of internal knowledge, phenomenon of attention decay, and representation of users. The demonstrated effects of control include targeted editing of the world model, reduced hallucination, improved stability of system prompts in long conversations, and better planning in multi-turn dialogue.

papers.title: Jointly Generating and Attributing Answers using Logits of Document-Identifier Tokens
papers.research_question: Can we leverage LLM’s predictions through token logits to jointly generate the answer to a query and ground it with documents in a context? This includes investigating whether token logits can represent document contribution.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LoDIT, a method for faithful attributed answer generation in RAG by leveraging document-identifier token logits during generation, with a joint fine-tuning strategy to debias logits and improve attribution.
papers.conclusion: LoDIT effectively leverages document identifier logits for faithful attribution, demonstrating improvements in trustworthiness, efficiency, and robustness in RAG settings.
papers.key_findings:
LoDIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models on the Trust-Align benchmark, improving trustworthiness metrics like TRUST score.
LoDIT enhances citation groundedness (F1GC) compared to baselines, indicating better attribution faithfulness.
The method is efficient, adding minimal latency during inference by jointly generating and attributing answers.
LoDIT is robust to variations in document ordering and identifier token selection after training.
Experiments show consistent improvements across multiple datasets (ASQA, QAMPARI, ELI5) in answer correctness and attribution quality.
future_direction: Extending LoDIT toward an end-to-end learnable token-level and statement-level attribution.
Investigating how the logit-based approach could be extended to answer token selection and mitigate other types of bias.
papers.abstract: Despite their impressive performances, Large Language Models (LLMs) remain prone to hallucination, which critically undermines their trustworthiness. While most of the previous work focused on tackling answer and attribution correctness, a recent line of work investigated faithfulness, with a focus on leveraging internal model signals to reflect a model's actual decision-making process while generating the answer. Nevertheless, these methods induce additional latency and have shown limitations in directly aligning token generation with attribution generation. In this paper, we introduce LoDIT, a method that jointly generates and faithfully attributes answers in RAG by leveraging specific token logits during generation. It consists of two steps: (1) marking the documents with specific token identifiers and then leveraging the logits of these tokens to estimate the contribution of each document to the answer during generation, and (2) aggregating these contributions into document attributions. Experiments on a trustworthiness-focused attributed text-generation benchmark, Trust-Align, show that LoDIT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models on several metrics. Finally, an in-depth analysis of LoDIT shows both its efficiency in terms of latency and its robustness in different settings.

papers.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
papers.research_question: How do deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLMs compared to truthful ones, and when and how do these representations flip?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts in early-to-mid layers, identifiable via SAEs, and identifies specific SAE features that flip under deception, providing a basis for deception detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals layer- and feature-level signatures of deception in LLMs, providing a basis for future deception detection and model editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The model's True/False output is linearly predictable from internal activations under all instructional conditions.
Deceptive instructions induce large representational shifts compared to truthful/neutral ones, concentrated in early-to-mid layers.
These shifts are detectable even on complex datasets where PCA fails.
Specific SAE features are highly sensitive to deceptive instructions and show near-binary activation patterns.
Truthful and neutral representations are similar, while deceptive ones are distinct.
papers.limitation:
Confined to English declaratives, frozen model weights, and linear probes.
Does not test causal interventions (e.g., activation patching) nor adversarial prompt recombinations.
Evaluation data are labeled for binary factuality only, not graded truth scales or multilingual settings.
future_direction: Extend to graded truth scales
Extend to multilingual settings
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tend to follow maliciously crafted instructions to generate deceptive responses, posing safety challenges. How deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLM compared to truthful ones remains poorly understood beyond output analysis. To bridge this gap, we investigate when and how these representations ``flip'', such as from truthful to deceptive, under deceptive versus truthful/neutral instructions. Analyzing the internal representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct on a factual verification task, we find the model's instructed True/False output is predictable via linear probes across all conditions based on the internal representation. Further, we use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to show that the Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers and detectable even on complex datasets. We also identify specific SAE features highly sensitive to deceptive instruction and use targeted visualizations to confirm distinct truthful/deceptive representational subspaces. % Our analysis pinpoints layer-wise and feature-level correlates of instructed dishonesty, offering insights for LLM detection and control. Our findings expose feature- and layer-level signatures of deception, offering new insights for detecting and mitigating instructed dishonesty in LLMs.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
papers.research_question: How can we rigorously evaluate the faithfulness of natural language explanations that claim individual neurons in a language model represent a concept?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework with observational and intervention modes to evaluate natural language explanations of neurons, and applies it to show that GPT-4-generated explanations for GPT-2 XL neurons have low faithfulness and causal efficacy.
papers.conclusion: Natural language may not be the best medium for model explanations due to vagueness and ambiguity, and neurons may not be the optimal unit of analysis; structured formalisms and analysis of neuron groups are promising alternatives.
papers.key_findings:
Even among the top 0.6% of neurons with GPT-4 explanation scores ≥0.8, explanations achieve only 0.64 precision and 0.50 recall.
Intervention-based evaluation shows GPT-4 explanations have little to no causal efficacy, performing similarly to random baselines.
Individual neurons are not effective causal mediators; causal effects require aggregating over many neurons, especially in early MLP layers.
Natural language explanations are often vague and ambiguous, making them unreliable for technical decision-making.
The GPT-4 score used by Bills et al. (2023) is insensitive to Type I errors and does not guarantee faithful explanations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on GPT-2 XL; results may not extend directly to other architectures.
Faithful explanations could be used for malicious manipulations of models.
future_direction: Use structured formalisms (e.g., programming languages) instead of natural language for explanations.
Analyze groups of neurons or other network components (e.g., attention heads, residual streams) as units of analysis.
Conduct similar evaluations on other model architectures.
papers.abstract: Natural language is an appealing medium for explaining how large language models process and store information, but evaluating the faithfulness of such explanations is challenging. To help address this, we develop two modes of evaluation for natural language explanations that claim individual neurons represent a concept in a text input. In the *observational mode*, we evaluate claims that a neuron a activates on all and only input strings that refer to a concept picked out by the proposed explanation E. In the *intervention mode*, we construe E as a claim that neuron a is a causal mediator of the concept denoted by E. We apply our framework to the GPT-4-generated explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons of Bills et al. (2023) and show that even the most confident explanations have high error rates and little to no causal efficacy. We close the paper by critically assessing whether natural language is a good choice for explanations and whether neurons are the best level of analysis.

papers.title: Hierarchical interpretations for neural network predictions
papers.research_question: How can we provide hierarchical interpretations of deep neural network predictions to improve model transparency and trust?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Agglomerative Contextual Decomposition (ACD), a method that produces hierarchical interpretations of DNN predictions by clustering input features and quantifying each cluster's contribution, enabling better model understanding and trust.
papers.conclusion: ACD is a novel hierarchical interpretation algorithm that captures non-linear feature interactions in DNN predictions, improves user trust and model selection, and is robust to adversarial noise.
papers.key_findings:
ACD produces hierarchical visualizations that can diagnose incorrect predictions and identify dataset bias, such as a model associating hockey skates with the class 'puck'.
Human experiments show that ACD helps users identify the more accurate of two models and increases their trust in a model's outputs compared to prior interpretation methods.
ACD's hierarchical clustering is robust to adversarial perturbations, suggesting it captures fundamental input features rather than spurious noise.
The method generalizes contextual decomposition (CD) from LSTMs to arbitrary DNN architectures, including CNNs.
ACD can extract top-scoring phrases of varying lengths that are semantically meaningful, such as positive and negative sentiment phrases from text.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved impressive predictive performance due to their ability to learn complex, non-linear relationships between variables. However, the inability to effectively visualize these relationships has led to DNNs being characterized as black boxes and consequently limited their applications. To ameliorate this problem, we introduce the use of hierarchical interpretations to explain DNN predictions through our proposed method, agglomerative contextual decomposition (ACD). Given a prediction from a trained DNN, ACD produces a hierarchical clustering of the input features, along with the contribution of each cluster to the final prediction. This hierarchy is optimized to identify clusters of features that the DNN learned are predictive. Using examples from Stanford Sentiment Treebank and ImageNet, we show that ACD is effective at diagnosing incorrect predictions and identifying dataset bias. Through human experiments, we demonstrate that ACD enables users both to identify the more accurate of two DNNs and to better trust a DNN's outputs. We also find that ACD's hierarchy is largely robust to adversarial perturbations, implying that it captures fundamental aspects of the input and ignores spurious noise.

papers.title: Enhancing Trust in AI: A Comparative Study of Explainable Machine Learning Models for Critical Decision-Making
papers.research_question: This study evaluates explainable machine learning models in financial applications, focusing on their ability to balance predictive accuracy with interpretability while addressing challenges in fraud detection and digital transactions.
papers.core_contribution: The study demonstrates that explainable AI techniques, such as LIME and SHAP, enhance trust and transparency in critical decision-making by balancing predictive accuracy with interpretability, particularly in financial applications.
papers.conclusion: Explainable AI is essential for responsible AI deployment in critical applications, bridging the gap between accuracy and interpretability to foster trust and regulatory compliance.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid models achieve 92% of deep neural network performance while improving interpretability scores by 40%.
Post-hoc explanations add marginal computational latency (under 15ms per prediction), making them viable for real-time systems.
Domain-specific visualization dashboards increase stakeholder trust by 58% compared to raw explanation outputs.
In user studies, domain experts expressed greater confidence in decisions made by interpretable models, even when marginally less accurate.
SHAP and LIME explanations corroborated feature importance rankings from interpretable models, increasing confidence in black-box models' predictions.
papers.limitation:
Achieving a balance between predictive accuracy and interpretability remains complex, as highly accurate models are often less transparent.
Generating explanations that are both faithful to the underlying model and accessible to diverse user groups requires careful design and evaluation.
future_direction: Developing adaptive explanation systems that tailor outputs to the expertise and needs of different stakeholders.
Conducting longitudinal studies that assess the impact of repeated human-AI interactions on trust and decision quality.
Co-designing AI solutions with domain experts to advance explainable and trustworthy AI.
papers.abstract: The integration of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in high-stakes decision making systems has become critical for fostering trust and regulatory compliance across industries. This study evaluates explainable machine learning models in f inancial applications, focusing on their ability to balance predictive accuracy with interpretability while addressing emerging challenges in fraud detection and digital transactions [1, 2]. Through comparative analysis of techniques like LIME and SHAP, we demonstrate how model-agnostic explanation frameworks enhance transparency in black-box systems without compromising performance. Our findings reveal that strategic implementation of XAI principles improves human-AI collaboration in sensitive domains, particularly when combined with real-time monitoring approaches [3]. The research contributes actionable insights for developing auditable AI systems that meet evolving regulatory requirements and organizational risk management frameworks.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: When Models Examine Themselves: Vocabulary-Activation Correspondence in Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does self-referential vocabulary produced by large language models correspond to their internal activation dynamics during self-examination?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Pull Methodology to elicit extended self-examination and shows that self-referential vocabulary tracks internal activation dynamics, with a specific direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential processing and can causally steer introspective output.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential vocabulary in transformer models corresponds to internal activation dynamics during self-examination, and this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing and replicates across different architectures.
papers.key_findings:
The Pull Methodology produces systematic, frame-dependent self-referential output across frontier models.
A direction in early layers (6.25% depth in Llama, 12.5% in Qwen) distinguishes self-referential processing and is orthogonal to the refusal direction.
This direction can be used to steer introspective vocabulary density in Llama models.
Vocabulary like 'loop' correlates with activation autocorrelation during self-referential processing, but not in descriptive contexts.
The correspondence replicates in Qwen with different vocabulary-metric pairings, indicating architecture-specific but principle-general behavior.
papers.limitation:
Closed-model / open-weight gap: behavioral study on closed-source models but mechanistic study on open-weight models, limiting direct verification.
No Qwen causal verification: correspondence in Qwen is correlational without steering experiments.
Correspondence is not self-knowledge; it tracks computational state without implying awareness or understanding.
Study design and hypothesis structure: vocabulary categories were not pre-registered, though tested with controls.
Quantisation: experiments used 4-bit quantisation, which may affect activation dynamics.
future_direction: Replicating correspondence in a third model family (e.g., Gemma, Mistral).
Investigating compressed vocabulary at steering strength 3.0 for more direct mechanism description.
Decomposing the effect to individual attention heads within the hotspot layer.
papers.abstract: Large language models produce rich introspective language when prompted for self-examination, but whether this language reflects internal computation or sophisticated confabulation has remained unclear. We show that self-referential vocabulary tracks concurrent activation dynamics, and that this correspondence is specific to self-referential processing. We introduce the Pull Methodology, a protocol that elicits extended self-examination through format engineering, and use it to identify a direction in activation space that distinguishes self-referential from descriptive processing in Llama 3.1. The direction is orthogonal to the known refusal direction, localised at 6.25% of model depth, and causally influences introspective output when used for steering. When models produce "loop" vocabulary, their activations exhibit higher autocorrelation (r = 0.44, p = 0.002); when they produce "shimmer" vocabulary under steering, activation variability increases (r = 0.36, p = 0.002). Critically, the same vocabulary in non-self-referential contexts shows no activation correspondence despite nine-fold higher frequency. Qwen 2.5-32B, with no shared training, independently develops different introspective vocabulary tracking different activation metrics, all absent in descriptive controls. The findings indicate that self-report in transformer models can, under appropriate conditions, reliably track internal computational states. Guided repro: https://github.com/patternmatcher/TRACE-REPRO

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do distributional and mechanistic factors determine a language model's behavior when there is a conflict between memorized facts and in-context information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies specific attention heads that control the use of memorized vs. in-context information and shows that scaling these heads at runtime can dynamically control model behavior without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that frequency and specific attention heads influence factual recall and provides a proof of concept for controlling model behavior dynamically at runtime.
papers.key_findings:
The frequency of the country and in-context city in pretraining data affects the model's tendency to use memorized vs. in-context information.
Larger models are more likely to use memorized answers, especially for frequent terms.
Individual attention heads can be identified that promote either memorized or in-context answers.
Scaling down a memory head can increase the rate of in-context answers to 88% on the world capitals task.
The memory head promotes geography-related tokens, indicating domain specificity, and does not generalize well to other factual domains.
papers.limitation: The dataset used is templated and limited to the domain of country-capital relationships, so findings may not generalize to arbitrary contexts.
future_direction: Developing more general techniques for controlling the use of context vs. memorized information in arbitrary tasks.
Discovering more general mechanisms beyond domain-specific heads.
papers.abstract: Language Models (LMs) often must integrate facts they memorized in pretraining with new information that appears in a given context. These two sources can disagree, causing competition within the model, and it is unclear how an LM will resolve the conflict. On a dataset that queries for knowledge of world capitals, we investigate both distributional and mechanistic determinants of LM behavior in such situations. Specifically, we measure the proportion of the time an LM will use a counterfactual prefix (e.g., “The capital of Poland is London”) to overwrite what it learned in pretraining (“Warsaw”). On Pythia and GPT2, the training frequency of both the query country (”Poland”) and the in-context city (”London”) highly affect the models’ likelihood of using the counterfactual. We then use head attribution to identify individual attention heads that either promote the memorized answer or the in-context answer in the logits. By scaling up or down the value vector of these heads, we can control the likelihood of using the in-context answer on new data. This method can increase the rate of generating the in-context answer to 88% of the time simply by scaling a single head at runtime. Our work contributes to a body of evidence showing that we can often localize model behaviors to specific components and provides a proof of concept for how future methods might control model behavior dynamically at runtime.

papers.title: SocioProbe: What, When, and Where Language Models Learn about Sociodemographics
papers.research_question: What, when, and where do language models learn about sociodemographics? Specifically, to what extent do they encode such knowledge, how much pre-training data is needed, where in the model is it located, does it differ in multilingual models, and what is the effect of supplementary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SocioProbe, a method to probe sociodemographic knowledge in PLMs, and finds that such knowledge is encoded but is more diffuse than lower-level linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: We find that sociodemographic knowledge is located in PLMs, but much more diffuse than lower-level aspects. We hope that our findings will fuel further research towards human-like language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode sociodemographic knowledge, but the extent varies across models and textual domains.
Sociodemographic knowledge requires large amounts of pre-training data and learning curves do not flatten.
Sociodemographic knowledge is less localized in model layers compared to syntactic knowledge (e.g., CoLA).
In multilingual models, the localization of sociodemographic knowledge is similar to monolingual models.
Supplementary training on intermediate tasks (STILTs) can overwrite sociodemographic knowledge in the higher layers.
papers.limitation:
Predictive methods can result in potentially harmful applications (dual use).
Gender is modeled as a binary variable, not reflecting the full spectrum of identities.
Models are limited to single-GPU, general-purpose pre-trained models; results may differ for larger or domain-specific models.
future_direction: Extend analysis to languages other than English
Explore models with different architectures and pre-training objectives
Investigate sociodemographic knowledge in larger and domain-specific models
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) have outperformed other NLP models on a wide range of tasks. Opting for a more thorough understanding of their capabilities and inner workings, researchers have established the extend to which they capture lower-level knowledge like grammaticality, and mid-level semantic knowledge like factual understanding. However, there is still little understanding of their knowledge of higher-level aspects of language. In particular, despite the importance of sociodemographic aspects in shaping our language, the questions of whether, where, and how PLMs encode these aspects, e.g., gender or age, is still unexplored. We address this research gap by probing the sociodemographic knowledge of different single-GPU PLMs on multiple English data sets via traditional classifier probing and information-theoretic minimum description length probing. Our results show that PLMs do encode these sociodemographics, and that this knowledge is sometimes spread across the layers of some of the tested PLMs. We further conduct a multilingual analysis and investigate the effect of supplementary training to further explore to what extent, where, and with what amount of pre-training data the knowledge is encoded. Our overall results indicate that sociodemographic knowledge is still a major challenge for NLP. PLMs require large amounts of pre-training data to acquire the knowledge and models that excel in general language understanding do not seem to own more knowledge about these aspects.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
